title: Discounting and the mid-year convention
objectives: Answer out loud: What does the mid-year convention do and why?

steps.body: End-of-year convention assumes each year's cash arrives on Dec 31.
Mid-year convention assumes cash arrives evenly through the year, so discount periods are 0.5, 1.5, 2.5…

blocks.template: With the mid-year convention, year 1 cash flow is discounted {{1}} years

blocks.title: Why use the mid-year convention?
blocks.teaser: Businesses earn cash throughout the year, not in one lump at year-end.
blocks.body: Businesses earn cash throughout the year, not in one lump at year-end. Mid-year is more realistic and gives a slightly higher value.

blocks.title: How does the mid-year convention affect terminal value?
blocks.teaser: For perpetuity growth TV (built from cash flows), use the mid-year discount period (e.g., 4.5 for a 5-year model).
blocks.body:
For perpetuity growth TV (built from cash flows), use the mid-year discount period (e.g., 4.5 for a 5-year model). For exit-multiple TV (an assumed sale at year-end), discount the full 5 years.

**Interview answer:** "Perpetuity growth TV uses the mid-year period because it's built from cash flows; exit-multiple TV assumes a sale at year-end, so it uses the full period."

blocks.prompt: 5-year DCF with the mid-year convention. Which discount period is used for an exit-multiple terminal value?
blocks.explanation: An exit multiple assumes a sale at year-end, so discount the full 5 years. A perpetuity-growth TV uses the mid-year period (4.5).

blocks.title: What's a stub period?
blocks.teaser: If the valuation date is mid-year (say, Sept 30), the first projected period is only a partial year.
blocks.body: If the valuation date is mid-year (say, Sept 30), the first projected period is only a partial year. You include only the remaining cash flow for that stub and adjust all later discount periods accordingly.
